turns.text: hey, how's your evening treating you?

Pretty low-key so far. I went for a short walk earlier while the weather was still decent, then came back and put on some chillhop while tidying up. Now I’m just deciding whether to start something or keep doing nothing on purpose.

How about you—how’s your evening going?

Mine’s been good, low-key too. I made some tea and put on a lo-fi playlist, and I was reading a little earlier. But now I’m kind of in that same in-between mode where I could start something else or just let the evening be soft and unplanned.

Doing nothing on purpose is honestly underrated. Do you have a show or book in mind if you decide to start something?

Tea and lo-fi sounds like a solid evening. And yeah, “soft and unplanned” is a good way to put it—sometimes the best option is just leaving the night alone.

If I do start something, I’ve been going back and forth between finally trying *Severance* or just rewatching *The Good Place* for comfort. I’m leaning comfort if I’m being honest. I don’t have a book going right now, which I’ve been meaning to fix.

What were you reading earlier? Anything you’d recommend?

Comfort rewatch sounds very valid. *Severance* is one I’d probably save for a night I want to be pulled in, not wind down.

Earlier I was reading *A Psalm for the Wild-Built* by Becky Chambers. It’s short, gentle, and thoughtful—kind of a hopeful solarpunk novella about a tea monk and a robot having philosophical conversations. Not plot-heavy in a stressful way, more like a quiet character piece. It’s been perfect for evenings when I want to read but don’t want anything too demanding.

I’d definitely recommend it if you’re looking for something warm and low-pressure to get back into reading. Have you read any Becky Chambers before, or do you usually go for different stuff?

That sounds really lovely—a tea monk and a robot having philosophical conversations is exactly the kind of premise I could go for right now. I haven’t read any Becky Chambers yet, but I’ve seen her recommended enough that your description might finally bump it up my list.

I’ve been out of the reading habit for a bit. When I do read, I tend to drift toward nonfiction about tech/internet history, old media, or design, but for fiction I like quiet, character-driven stuff—sometimes sci-fi, sometimes just contemporary that doesn’t feel too harsh.

Do you usually lean toward that gentle/cozy speculative vibe, or are you more all over the place with reading?

I’m a little all over the place, but I do gravitate toward the gentle side for fiction. If a book feels too sharp or stressful, I’m less likely to finish it these days. Cozy speculative stuff has been a nice sweet spot, but I also like quiet contemporary novels and the occasional weird nonfiction dive.

Your nonfiction taste sounds very aligned with my internet rabbit holes. I go down a lot of rabbit holes about obscure music histories, old internet lore, lost media, weird local history—so any book that scratches that itch is dangerous for my focus.

Do you have a recent-ish read or rabbit hole that really stuck with you, especially in internet history or old media?

Not a book, but a rabbit hole that really stuck with me recently is the history of Muzak and background music in public spaces. I’d always just thought of it as elevator music, but it was originally engineered with this whole philosophy about mood, productivity, and making spaces feel controlled. And then it became this accidental soundtrack for malls, grocery stores, and waiting rooms.

It connects weirdly well with the dead mall nostalgia stuff for me—like, part of why those spaces feel haunted is because the faint music is gone, but you can almost still hear the ghost of it. I also go down old-internet rabbit holes a lot: early web design, Flash sites, Geocities remnants, lost media resurfacing. The Internet Archive is dangerous for my attention span.

What about you—any weird nonfiction dive or internet rabbit hole you still think about?

That Muzak history really is one of those things that permanently changes how you hear a space. I love the way you connected it to dead malls too—like the silence is just the music turned down, not gone. It gives those places a strange afterimage quality.

For me, I still think about a few old lost media and early internet rabbit holes. The whole “Everyone Knows That” search stuck with me: years of people trying to identify a short, catchy song snippet from an old recording, and eventually it gets traced to something completely obscure. It wasn’t about the song being important—it was about a half-remembered sound becoming this shared memory itch the internet collectively refused to let stay lost.

Early Geocities and webring preservation is another one. There’s something almost tender about recovering these little hand-built, personal corners of the internet, half-broken MIDI and all. It makes me weirdly nostalgic for spaces that were never meant to be permanent.

Do you find the Muzak history more eerie, or weirdly comforting? I keep going back and forth on it.

That “afterimage quality” is exactly it. I’m going to be thinking about that phrase.

For me, Muzak history is both eerie and comforting, almost at the same time. The eerie part is how intentional it was: it wasn’t just background noise, it was designed to shape mood, pacing, even the way people shopped or worked. So a dead mall with the music gone feels less like simple decay and more like a machine that kept running long after its original purpose faded.

But the comforting part is the residue—the dry fountain, the dated tile, the memory of that faint, hollow instrumental sound. It’s like walking through a shared cultural dream nobody fully remembers agreeing to. I don’t find it threatening, just wistful.

That “Everyone Knows That” search is such a good example of the same impulse from a different angle: not preserving the object, but refusing to let the half-memory die. It’s less about the song than about the itch.

Are you more drawn to the hunt/identification side of lost media—the mystery—or to preservation efforts like Geocities archiving?
